questiontext.text: In an undirected graph, a connected component is best defined as:

answer.text: A maximal set of vertices that are all mutually reachable

feedback.text: Correct — a maximal mutually-reachable vertex set.
No — a component is a set of vertices, not a single path.

answer.text: The set of all edges incident to a vertex

feedback.text: No — that is a vertex's adjacency, not a component.

answer.text: A cycle that visits every vertex once

feedback.text: No — that describes a Hamiltonian cycle.

generalfeedback.text: A connected component is a maximal subset of vertices such that a path exists between every pair; "maximal" means it cannot be extended by adding more reachable vertices.

questiontext.text: What is the standard traversal-based method to find all connected components?

answer.text: Run BFS or DFS from each not-yet-visited vertex; each traversal marks one component

feedback.text: Correct — one traversal per unvisited start yields one component.

answer.text: Run a single BFS from vertex 0 only

feedback.text: No — one BFS reaches only the component containing vertex 0.
No — shortest paths are unnecessary; plain BFS/DFS suffices.

answer.text: Sort the edges and scan them once

feedback.text: No — sorting edges alone does not group vertices into components.

generalfeedback.text: Loop over all vertices; whenever you hit an unvisited one, launch BFS/DFS to mark its whole component, then increment the component count.

questiontext.text: Using BFS/DFS with adjacency lists, the time to find all connected components is:

feedback.text: Correct — each vertex and edge is examined a constant number of times.
That would hold for an adjacency matrix, not adjacency lists.
No — no priority queue or sorting is involved.
No — that is far more work than a linear traversal requires.

generalfeedback.text: Every vertex is visited once and every edge traversed a constant number of times, giving linear O(V + E) time.

questiontext.text: Besides BFS/DFS, which data structure is commonly used to maintain connected components as edges are added?

feedback.text: Correct — union-find merges sets as edges connect vertices.
No — heaps order by key; they do not track connectivity.

answer.text: A hash table of edge weights

feedback.text: No — that stores weights, not component membership.

answer.text: A balanced binary search tree of vertices

feedback.text: No — a BST orders keys but does not group connected sets.

generalfeedback.text: Union-Find with union-by-rank and path compression answers "same component?" and merges components in near-constant amortized time, ideal for incremental edge insertion.

questiontext.text: The term "connected components" (as opposed to strongly connected components) applies to undirected graphs.

feedback.text: Correct — plain connected components are defined on undirected graphs.
Undirected graphs have connected components; directed graphs have strongly connected components.

questiontext.text: A graph is called connected when it has exactly one connected component.

feedback.text: Correct — one component covering all vertices means the graph is connected.
By definition a connected graph consists of a single component.

questiontext.text: A maximal set of mutually reachable vertices in an undirected graph is called a connected ______ (one English word).

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about connected components are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Each vertex belongs to exactly one connected component

feedback.text: Yes — components partition the vertex set.

answer.text: BFS and DFS discover the same components

feedback.text: Yes — the components are a property of the graph, not the traversal order.

answer.text: A graph with n vertices always has exactly one component

feedback.text: No — a graph can have many components, up to n isolated vertices.

answer.text: Finding components requires sorting the vertices first

feedback.text: No — a simple BFS/DFS sweep needs no sorting.

generalfeedback.text: Components partition the vertices; every vertex is in exactly one. Both BFS and DFS find the same partition in O(V + E) with no sorting required.
